doc.title: Mike Wofford interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998

chapter: San Diego and the state of jazz
title: Why a serious jazz player has to go to New York
summary: Though he never lived in New York, he explains it is the proving ground, and west coast players like Gordon, Mingus and Coleman became known only after going east.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: So you’ve never done the New York thing?

No. I spent a lot of time in New York. I’ve never actually resided there. I’ve been there for weeks at a time on different recording projects or playing. I’ve always regretted that and I always advise young players if they’re really serious about doing something, sooner or later they have to deal with New York. They have to take that step and do it. And that discourages a lot of them right there. But I firmly believe that New York is the proving ground where ultimately you have to be able to hold your own, if you’re looking for the kind of recognition and opportunities that are going to help build a career. Now you can play the music for the sheer satisfaction of playing the music, and even maybe make some kind of a living at it if you can also do other things as well, you know, play shows and do accompanying, which I’ve done quite a bit of over the years. You can do all of

those things anywhere, virtually, if it’s an area of any size. But if you’re serious about carving a place for yourself in the scheme of things, it has to be done in New York City. And it doesn’t happen in Los Angeles, and it doesn’t happen — now people can, once they’ve arrived in New York, can go anywhere and carry that attaché with them. I mean I know great New York players who now live in Santa Fe, New Mexico or wherever, but they will always be thought of as New York players. It doesn’t matter. But if you haven’t made that step there then it’s very difficult. There are so many wonderful players on the west coast who just languished out here because there isn’t the press out here, there isn’t the springboard to Europe — just geographically you’re at a disadvantage being on the west coast. There’s Asia obviously but still it’s really the proximity to Europe and the ability to travel over there, more so now than ever, I mean it’s really true today, that I think many musicians depend on Europe for a big part of their employment each year, and for outlets for playing. But a lot of great players came from the west, went to New York, changed the music in New York, and are always thought of as New Yorkers, like Dexter Gordon and Charlie Mingus and Ornette Coleman, and on and on. But those were all Los Angeles players. But had they stayed in Los Angeles—
You wouldn’t know their names, that’s right.
